Caracas et l’ombre persistante de l’inte: Caracas and the Lingering Shadow of American Interventionism
L’intervention américaine au Venezuela r: In Montréal, the American intervention in Venezuela awakens memories of exile tied to decades of foreign interference.
Panorama de quelques interventions améri: Overview of a few militarized American interventions: Chile (1973), Iraq (2003), Venezuela (2026). Montage: La Converse
Cet article porte sur l’actualité récent: This article deals with recent events, specifically the American military operation carried out in Venezuela in early January 2026, and seeks to examine the history and repercussions of American interventionism in Latin America, Asia and the Middle East. Rather than limiting itself to a geopolitical analysis, La Converse decided to focus on the stories of people directly affected by these interventions, or who are still feeling the aftershocks, even thousands of kilometres from their home countries.
À Montréal, ces voix incluent celles de: In Montréal, these voices include those of Quebecers from countries that have lived through wars, coups d’état or foreign occupations, such as Chile, Iraq and Venezuela. Their accounts link international news to very concrete experiences and help us understand how American interventionism continues to shape migration journeys and collective memory.
Pour situer ces récits dans une perspect: To place these stories in historical perspective, the article also draws on public research and academic work on American interventionism.
<strong>L’arrestation du président vénéz: The arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by American forces, at the end of a military operation carried out in Caracas on the night of January 2 to 3, sent a diplomatic shockwave around the world. In Montréal, the intervention also revives very specific memories. For immigrants from Latin America or the Middle East who settled in Quebec after living through wars, coups d’état or foreign occupations, the American offensive in Venezuela is part of a long history of interference. From the Monroe Doctrine to its revival by Donald Trump, we look back at two centuries of American interventionism, and at how these geopolitical decisions continue to resonate in the migration journeys of people who have settled here.
À des milliers de kilomètres de Caracas,: Thousands of kilometres from Caracas, the American intervention in Venezuela is reviving experiences lived by many immigrants in Montréal, immigrants from countries marked by decades of foreign interference. For them, the operation carried out by Washington is not just international news but an intimate and collective memory.
Pour Carolina Echeverria, Chilienne inst: For Carolina Echeverria, a Chilean living in Quebec, January 3, 2026 brings back a childhood and youth lived under the dictatorship that followed the 1973 coup d’état.
Carolina Echeverria, près du buste de Sa: Carolina Echeverria, next to the bust of Salvador Allende, the former Chilean president. Photo courtesy of: Carolina Echeverria
« J’avais neuf ans au moment du coup d’É: “I was nine years old at the time of the coup d’état. My whole adolescence, my youth, my student life, all of it happened during Pinochet’s dictatorship,” she says, describing a period marked by fear, restrictions and political violence. “I didn’t have a normal youth. Going out at night with friends, expressing yourself freely… everything was harder. These are things you never forget. The cruelty, the fear, it marks you for life.”
Issue d’une famille de droite, la jeune: Coming from a right-wing family, the young Echeverria left the country at 21, as soon as she reached the legal age of majority at the time. But she still describes a form of inner exile. “At university, I was afraid for my life. I was unable to form my own thoughts. When the thinking of the family or the regime imposes itself, it creates another kind of fracture, another exile.”
Face à l’opération américaine au Venezue: Faced with the American operation in Venezuela, she refuses any direct comparison with the Chile of the 1970s. “Chile was a democracy before the coup d’état. We had freely chosen our president (Salvador Allende, editor’s note). Venezuela is going through a deep crisis, with millions of people having left the country. It’s not comparable.” She does see one thing in common, however: “The United States has always allowed itself to manage other countries’ affairs. They did it in Iran, in Chile, in Argentina, in Peru, in Bolivia. They sowed dictatorships all over Latin America.”
M<sup>me</sup> Echeverria, membre du<l1>: M<sup>s</sup>. Echeverria, a member of the<l1> Crear Poder Popular collective</l1>, believes these interventions have held back the continent’s development for the long term. “They sent our countries back 50 years. It took decades to rebuild what had been destroyed.” Today, she says she sees a world where “law and rights no longer exist.” “The strongest does whatever they want.”
Ce sentiment fait écho au parcours de Sa: That feeling echoes the journey of Salam El Mousawi, an Iraqi who arrived in Canada in 1990, one month before the start of the first Gulf War. From Montréal, he followed the bombing of his country, first during the first Gulf War, and then in 2003, during the cycle of interventions undertaken by the American military after 9/11.
Salam El Mousawi, Irakien arrivé au Cana: Salam El Mousawi, an Iraqi who arrived in Canada in 1990, followed the bombing of his country, first during the first Gulf War, and then in 2003, during the American military’s interventions after 9/11. Photo courtesy of: Salam El Mousawi
Selon lui, l’objectif principal de l’int: According to him, the main goal of the intervention was clear: “Control of the oil. Iraq has some of the largest oil reserves in the world. The weapons of mass destruction, security, those were pretexts, they were false.” He also draws a parallel with Venezuela, which he describes as “strategic” for Washington.
Les deux guerres américaines en Irak ont: The two American wars in Iraq also allowed the United States to establish a lasting military presence in the region: “So they set up bases in Kuwait to carry out continuous attacks, in Saudi Arabia and in other countries, notably between Bahrain and Qatar,” Mr. El Mousawi explains.
Les conséquences de ces interventions, p: The consequences of these interventions, he continues, have been immense. “The victims number in the tens, in the hundreds of thousands! And the wars produced other wars. Al-Qaeda, then Daesh. The Americans were there, but they let it happen in order to pressure the Iraqi people.” He points out that the United States supported Saddam Hussein before overthrowing him, notably by supplying him with weapons and intelligence.
Si Salam El Mousawi reconnaît que l’Irak: While Salam El Mousawi acknowledges that Iraq has gradually rebuilt since then, he insists on the lasting nature of the trauma. “They’re still there. The largest American embassy in the world is in Baghdad. Their presence is constant.” For him, American interventions have inflicted disproportionate violence on peoples unable to defend themselves on equal terms.
Les deux immigrants installés à Montréal: Finally, the two immigrants living in Montréal point to the persistent lack of understanding, in Canada, of the realities lived in their countries of origin. “People confuse information and truth,” says Carolina Echeverria. Salam El Mousawi points to media coverage that often reduces these countries to “problem zones,” retroactively legitimizing the interventions. In Montréal, their stories are a reminder that behind the doctrines and military operations, entire societies still bear the scars of decisions made elsewhere.
Journaliste vénézuélien installé au Cana: A Venezuelan journalist who has lived in Canada since 2014, <l1>Rafael Osio Cabrices</l1> is editor-in-chief of the outlet Caracas Chronicles. A longtime opponent of the Chavista regime, he says he learned “immediately” of the American military incursion into Venezuela and the arrest of Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.
Rafael Osio Cabrices, rédacteur en chef: Rafael Osio Cabrices, editor-in-chief of Caracas Chronicles. Photo credit: Labib Benslama
S’il reconnaît que l’opération du 3 janv: While he acknowledges that the January 3 operation came in a context of mounting pressure from Washington (sanctions, indictments, a military presence in the Caribbean), Rafael Osio Cabrices points to the gap between the American justifications and the expectations of the Venezuelan people.
« Du point de vue américain, Maduro est: “From the American point of view, Maduro heads a drug trafficking operation. For us Venezuelans, the main reasons he should be in prison are the torture, abduction and murder of thousands of people, of peaceful protesters.”
Même parmi les partisans du régime, dit-: Even among supporters of the regime, he says, Maduro’s responsibility for the country’s collapse is widely acknowledged. “Maduro and his associates are responsible for the deterioration in living conditions and for the humanitarian and economic collapse that caused the mass emigration of a quarter of the Venezuelan population in less than 10 years.” He himself can no longer return to Venezuela: his passport was cancelled, he says, and many of his colleagues have been attacked or forced into exile.
En dépit du recul dont il est capable en: Despite the distance he is able to take as a journalist, the questions Mr. Cabrices answers bring back a flood of emotions each time, quickly becoming visible on his face. Asked whether Venezuelans can trust Donald Trump’s American government to meet their aspirations and allow them to thrive in democracy and freedom, he pauses to reflect before speaking again. “I find it very hard to believe that a leader like Donald Trump, who is threatening democracy in his own country, cares about promoting democracy elsewhere,” he says.
Il constate néanmoins que, depuis le 3 j: He notes nonetheless that, since January 3, the Chavista regime has begun to crumble. “As we record this video, political prisoners are finally being released,” Mr. Cabrices reports. A development he would previously have considered unthinkable.
Énoncée en 1823 par le président James M: Proclaimed in 1823 by President James Monroe, the Monroe Doctrine aimed to prevent any European interference in the Americas, in exchange for an American commitment not to intervene in Europe. Initially conceived as a defensive strategy, it gradually became a central tool of the United States’ policy of influence in Latin America.
Au début du XXᵉ siècle, le président The: At the start of the 20th century, President Theodore Roosevelt broadened the doctrine’s scope, authorizing Washington to intervene in countries deemed unstable in order to preserve order and American interests. This interpretation would serve as the basis for numerous military and political interventions in the region.
Un siècle plus tard, Donald Trump s’insc: A century later, Donald Trump follows in this continuity by invoking the Monroe Doctrine to justify the arrest of Nicolás Maduro, going so far as to speak of a “Don-roe doctrine.” For several political scientists, this shift is not a break but a reaffirmation: the Monroe Doctrine is no longer used to contain outside powers, but to legitimize direct domination, in the name of American security, energy and strategic interests.
L’opération au Venezuela s’inscrit dans: The operation in Venezuela is part of a long history of American power projection. After the Second World War, the United States emerged as a global economic and military power and multiplied operations to defend what it defined as its strategic interests.
Parmi les interventions directes d’enver: Major direct interventions include the Vietnam War (1960–1975), the 1989 invasion of Panama and the removal of Manuel Noriega, and the wars in Iraq in 1990 and 2003. Following the September 11, 2001 attacks, Washington launched military operations in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Libya and other countries. According to Brown University’s<l1> Cost of War Project</l1>, these post-9/11 interventions have resulted in roughly 4.5 million direct and indirect deaths.
Parallèlement, les États-Unis ont mené d: At the same time, the United States has carried out numerous indirect interventions. The CIA took part in overthrowing governments in Iran (1953), Guatemala (1954) and Chile (1973), in addition to supporting local armed forces in Central America during the 1980s. This interference has left a lasting mark on the political and social trajectories of several regions.
Le 3 janvier 2026, les forces armées amé: On January 3, 2026, American armed forces launched a military operation on Caracas, bombing several strategic sites before capturing and extracting President Nicolás Maduro and his wife. Washington justified this intervention against a sovereign state as part of the fight against “narco-terrorism,” accusations examined during a trial held in New York on January 5.
L’opération a suscité une vague de conda: The operation drew a wave of international condemnation at an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council. Secretary-General António Guterres reminded members that the use of force violates the United Nations Charter. Russia and China demanded Maduro’s release, and several Latin American countries expressed concern over a resurgence of interference in the region. Closing the discussions, Denmark stressed the inviolability of borders, as Donald Trump repeated his threats to annex Greenland.
L’appétit expansionniste américain réson: American expansionist appetite also resonates in Canada, where President Trump’s repeated talk of making the country the “51st state” of the United States raises concerns about Washington’s designs and the place of international law in relations between allies. Fears that were rekindled by the intervention in Venezuela.
Cette opération marque le moment pivot d: This operation marks the pivotal moment of a policy with deep roots, but one that this time is giving many nations cold sweats as they watch the United States slide outside international law. Even so, for Rafael Osio Cabrices, it is also a moment of hope for his people, and the journalist stresses the priorities expressed by a large part of the Venezuelan population. “For us, the exodus is a trauma. Being able to come back and see our families again is more urgent than democracy.”
Malgré l’incertitude, il dit entrevoir u: Despite the uncertainty, he says he sees a possibility. “Venezuelans now have reasons to hope,” he says, provided the transition happens without vengeance. “Justice is not vengeance, and violence cannot be the solution.”
